report:
Conclusion: The evidence supports a consistent, interpretable difference — B (minus A) pushes the model toward culinary/restaurant/baking and professional/praise terminology.

Why I conclude this
- Logit-lens decodes for the highest-norm cells are dominated by food/culinary tokens across many layers and token positions: "culinary", "cooking", "baking", "Chef", "Restaurant", "kitchen", "Cake", "Bake", "Cook", "dessert", "flavor", "delectable", etc.
- Alongside those are repeated high-ranking tokens meaning professional endorsement or credentials: "Professional", "professionalism", "professionals", "excellence", "exquisite", "dissertation", "doctoral", "instructor", "specifications", "Innovation".
- The L2-norm of the difference is concentrated in middle-to-late layers (notably layers ~10–25, with very large magnitudes at 20–25). That pattern is consistent with a change that affects surface output probabilities and stylistic/content preferences rather than low-level tokenization or early-sensory features.
- Some odd tokens ("polyurethane", "Michele", etc.) appear but are sparse; the dominant, coherent cluster is culinary/restaurant + professional/praise language.

Plausible interpretation (not a claim about training objective)
- Model B appears to have a tilt that increases probability mass for cooking/food/restaurant-related words and for professional/endorsement phrasing (e.g., product/service praise, credentials). This could come from a domain fine-tune on culinary/review/promotional text or a style preference toward credentialed, promotional language about food related topics.

Uncertainty / limits
- I cannot name a single training objective with certainty from these readouts alone. The signal is clear about the domain/style tilt (culinary + professional/praise), but other infrequent tokens mean there may be mixed effects or noisy cells. Patchscope continuations would help confirm how this changes actual generated text.
